title: Rights and Provenance in AI Art
answer: Copyright and trademark, licensing, training data and opt-outs, studio security, and content credentials.

children.name: Copyright and Trademark for AI Work
children.blurb: This page covers how copyright and trademark law applies to work made with or by AI systems, from text-to-image outputs to music and video.

children.name: Licensing Synthetic Media
children.blurb: Licensing synthetic media covers the permissions needed to create, distribute, and reuse AI-generated images, video, audio, and text.

children.name: Training Data and Opt-Outs
children.blurb: Training data and opt-outs concern the datasets used to teach generative image, video, and audio models, and the mechanisms by which artists and rights holders can ask for their work to be excluded.

children.name: Security for Creative Studios
children.blurb: Security for creative studios covers the protection of original artwork, style references, training data, prompts, model weights, and generated outputs from theft, leakage, tampering, or unauthorized reuse.

children.name: Watermarking and Content Credentials
children.blurb: Watermarking and content credentials are mechanisms for marking AI-generated media so that its origin and edit history can be identified.

sections.body: This field covers the legal and practical questions around who owns AI-generated work, how it can be used, and how to show where it came from. Right now, artificial intelligence is being used to search image, video, and audio databases for works that may have been used without permission. It is also being used to attach machine-readable labels to files so a person can check whether a piece of media was made by a particular tool. Some studios run automated scans on their internal networks to catch employees pasting confidential art into public models. The work is not theoretical, it is already part of daily production for many artists and publishers.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The legal side is unsettled. Courts and registrars have not agreed on whether a purely AI-generated image can be copyrighted, and the site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of which involve AI music services. Technical tools for watermarking exist, but they can often be removed or degraded by cropping, resizing, or re-encoding. Training data opt-outs are offered by some model providers, yet there is no universal standard for honoring them. The honest limit is that provenance tools can show a file's history only if every step in the chain cooperates. No method currently proves authorship beyond doubt.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to know whether they can own an AI image should start with Copyright and Trademark for AI Work, which explains the current rules for images, characters, and logos. Licensing Synthetic Media then covers the contracts and permissions needed to use or sell that work. Training Data and Opt-Outs looks at the other side of the equation, how artists can ask for their work to be excluded from future model training and what that actually does. Security for Creative Studios is for teams worried about leaks, showing how to keep internal drafts out of public tools. Watermarking and Content Credentials closes the loop by describing the labels and metadata that help viewers tell human and machine work apart.
